GLM-5.3-Flash is the first natively multimodal model in Z.ai’s GLM-5 series. With 320B total parameters and just 18B active, it outperforms GLM-5.2 across benchmarks and real-world workloads at one-tenth the cost, while approaching Claude Opus 4.8 on coding and agentic benchmarks. Before release, Z.ai tested GLM-5.3-Flash anonymously as ox-alpha where it became the most popular model of the week. Key Features Agentic Coding : Built for sustained, multi-step coding in agent harnesses. Long Context : A 1M context window holds project-scale codebases and long-running sessions. Flexible Thinking : Reasoning is always on, with effort tunable per request across low, high, and max levels. Multimodal Input : Accepts image and video alongside text, for workflows that mix code with visual context. MIT Licensed Competitive performance at Flash cost Across six coding and agentic benchmarks, GLM-5.3-Flash consistently outperforms GLM-5.2, often by a wide margin: 63.4 vs. 46.2 on DeepSWE v1.1 and 48.8 vs. 26.2 on AutomationBench, while approaching Claude Opus 4.8 overall. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.1.1, it pushes the Pareto frontier at 57 points, a level of intelligence previously only available at roughly 10× the cost per task. Built for efficient inference GLM-5.3-Flash starts from a newly trained base model, with its architecture and training recipe redesigned around capability and efficiency. Compared with GLM-4.5, it has a similar total parameter count (320B vs. 355B) but nearly halves both the active parameters (18B vs. 32B) and the number of layers (45 vs. 92). models.name: Designed for greater capability, faster inference, higher throughput, and scaling to larger models.
models.description: Readme DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: Pushing the Limits of KV Cache Compression DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash is an advanced tool designed to enhance search capabilities, providing users with faster and more accurate results. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 552B backbone parameters and support for contexts of up to one million tokens. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash uses a Causal Encoder-Decoder (CED) design, stacking a 20-layer causal encoder on top of a 20-layer decoder for 40 Transformer layers total. Under CED, the decoder’s global KV cache is built by projecting the encoder’s final hidden states, instead of being computed from each decoder layer’s hidden states as it normally would be. As a result, only 8B parameters are active per token during prefill and 16B during decode , which cuts costs significantly for agentic workloads that process a lot of input. ￼ DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash builds on Compressed Sparse Attention 2 (CSA2) , where every attention layer runs in one of three fixed modes - Full , Reindex , or Reuse - letting layers share main KV, share indexer K, and recycle Top-K sparse-attention indices. In the decoder, a Hierarchical Sparse Indexer caps later indexing layers to a candidate pool built by the first Full Mode layer, so indexer cost at deeper layers stays bounded no matter how long the context gets. Together with FP4 main KV caching (E2M1 values, one E4M3 scale per 16 channels), this brings the global KV cache down to 890 bytes per token - about a quarter of DeepSeek-V4-Flash. models.name: A 4B decision model from Together AI for fast classification.
models.description: Readme Tev1 requires Ollama 0.35 or later. Tev1 is a family of experimental decision models from Together AI, fine-tuned from Qwen3.5 in 4B and 0.8B sizes. You give it a question and a set of options. It selects the answer based on likely outcome, and gives you the probability of each option. It’s meant for the fast classification work that TypeSafe’s Jev does, like routing a support ticket or checking a request against a policy. Models 4B ollama pull tev1:4b 0.8B ollama pull tev1:0.8b Highlights Three question types: Pick from a list, answer true or false, or place something on a rubric. Two sizes: The 4B model is the more accurate of the two. The 0.8B model is an 812MB download for tight memory budgets. Many questions per request: Ask up to 64 questions about the same text in one call. Open: The dataset builders and training scripts are MIT licensed. API Decision models use Ollama’s /v1/systemone endpoint, which follows TypeSafe’s Jev API. Put the text you want judged in state and your questions in questions . Ollama builds Tev1’s prompt for you. Field Description model tev1 (the 4B model) or tev1:0.8b state The text to judge. Use a string, or a JSON object or array for structured input. questions 1 to 64 named questions. Answers come back in the same order. keep_alive Optional. How long the model stays loaded after the request. Every question has a type , instructions , and usually criteria : Type criteria Answer fields choice An object mapping each option to a description. Use null to let the option name describe itself. choice , probabilities , confidence noul Optional. {"true": "...", "false": "..."} if you want to describe each side. noul , the probability that the answer is true score An array of level descriptions, lowest first. Levels are numbered from 0. score (the probability-weighted level), legend , probabilities , confidence Choice and score questions take 2 to 26 options. Tev1 was trained on 2 to 24, so stay in that range. confidence runs from 0 to 1

models.name: EmbeddingGemma 2 is a multimodal embedding model from Google built on the Gemma 4 architecture.
models.description: Readme EmbeddingGemma 2 is an open multimodal embedding model built by Google DeepMind which maps text (incl. code), images, video, and audio inputs—and combinations thereof—into a single, unified 768-dimensional vector space. The model has 740M total parameters, combining a 270M parameter text model with modular vision (170M) and audio (300M) encoders. Designed to run on consumer hardware such as mobile devices and laptops, EmbeddingGemma 2 delivers low-latency semantic representations for on-device applications, like search, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), classification, and clustering. EmbeddingGemma 2 builds upon the architectural and capability advancements of Gemma 4, offering several core features:  Native multimodality: Native multimodality: Unifies 4 modalities (text, images, video, and audio) in a single shared 768-dimensional embedding space. Multilinguality and code: EmbeddingGemma 2 understands 100+ languages, and achieves a ~14% improvement on code tasks relative to its predecessor.  Flexible footprint: Combines a 270M parameter text backbone (130M transformer + 140M embedder) with selectively loadable vision (170M) and audio (300M) encoders, allowing developers to load only the modalities required for their use case. Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL): Native support for truncated embeddings across 128d, 256d, 512d, and 768d, enabling up to a 6x reduction in vector storage costs with minimal impact on quality. Context length: 8K token context window, capable of processing minutes of audio or video. Task-steered representations: Uses lightweight text instruction prefixes to optimize embeddings for different tasks (search, classification, clustering, semantic similarity, etc.). models.description: Readme Nimble is a 9B decision model from Bespoke Labs, fine-tuned from Qwen3.5-9B. You send Nimble some text and a set of questions. It picks an answer for every question and gives you the probability of each allowed answer. Nimble reads the prompt once per question and scores the answer tokens directly. There’s no reasoning step. This is what makes it fast. ollama pull nimble Highlights Three question types: Pick from a list, answer true or false, or place something on a rubric. Many questions per request: Ask up to 64 questions about the same text in one call. Fast: Nimble answers in under 100ms on a MacBook Pro with an M5 Max. Trained on contrastive pairs: The two examples in a pair differ by one fact, and that fact flips the answer. Primary capabilities Token-efficient reasoning: Reaches comparable solution quality to leading open models using approximately 3x fewer inference-time reasoning tokens. Software engineering: Resolves real-world GitHub issues, operates in CLI and DevOps environments, and integrates directly with agentic coding harnesses. Code generation supported across languages. Agentic tool use: Long-horizon task completion, MCP-based tool integration, and browsing. Executes multi-step workflows from natural-language instructions. Reasoning (math and science): Graduate-level science problem solving, theorem proving, and applied mathematics. Reasoning quality transfers to debugging, planning, and self-correction during agentic execution. Model Overview Beam models are designed to deliver strong performance for areas such as agentic tool use, coding and general reasoning with an emphasis on token efficient usage. models.description: Readme Clef requires Ollama 0.35.1 or later. To use Clef in Ollama’s cloud, use Ollama 0.40.6 or later. Clef is a 27B decision model from Cloudflare, fine-tuned from Qwen3.8-27B. Clef reads text, JSON, and images. Images are scored together with the text. Clef uses the System One API through Ollama’s /v1/systemone endpoint. You can call it from the Ollama CLI, the Ollama Python and JavaScript libraries, or TypeSafe’s Python SDK. See clef-flash for a smaller, faster variant. ollama pull clef Or run it in Ollama’s cloud with a paid plan or usage credits . No download needed: ollama run clef:cloud --ask "Is a refund being requested?" < ticket.txt Highlights Multimodal: Decide over text, JSON, or images, such as screenshots, receipts, forms, and photos. One forward pass: Every option of every question is scored jointly in a single non-autoregressive pass. 64K context window: Twice the state Jev’s 32K window holds. Leading accuracy: Clef tops the Decision Index, Cloudflare’s leaderboard of decision models, and beats Jev on most of its suite. models.description: Readme Nimble v3 Requires Ollama 0.40.4 or later. Nimble v3 is a 9B decision model from Bespoke Labs, fine-tuned from Qwen3.5-9B. Give it the relevant facts and questions with defined answers. It returns probabilities for those answers, letting your application route a request, check a condition, or assign a rating. It scores candidate answer tokens directly, without generating a reasoning trace or a free-form response. Noncommercial use only. Nimble v3 is licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0 , unlike the earlier nimble release. The Qwen3.5-9B base is separately licensed under Apache 2.0. See the publisher’s license statement . ollama pull nimble-v3 Highlights Three question types: categorical choices, Boolean questions, and ordered rubric scores. Multiple questions per request: evaluate several aspects of the same input. 32K text context: up to 32,768 tokens, including the formatted questions. MLX and GGUF: automatic backend selection, with unquantized and smaller quantized variants available. API Send requests to Ollama’s /v1/systemone endpoint. Put the evidence in state and name each question in questions . Ollama formats the model’s prompt and returns an answers object using those names. Type Criteria Result choice Option names mapped to descriptions. choice names the selected option; probabilities gives each option’s probability. noul Optional descriptions for true and false . noul is the probability that the answer is true, from 0 to 1. score An array of level descriptions in ascending order. score is the probability-weighted level, numbered from 0; probabilities and legend describe the levels. Give it a repository task—investigating a bug, implementing a feature, or writing tests—and it can reason through the work and use tools across multiple turns. models.description: Readme Kev Kev is a family of text decision models from Jared Palmer . It reads a state and one or more typed questions, then scores the supplied answers in a forward pass. Use Ollama’s local /v1/systemone API for classification, yes/no decisions, and ordered scores. Kev does not generate text or accept images. Requires Ollama 0.40.4 or later. These tags use the Apple Silicon MLX runner and advertise the decision capability. Choose a model kev and kev:latest select kev:9b-nvfp4 . It is the default balance of quality, response time, and memory on the tested M5 Max. The 27B variants are the quality choices; the 0.8B variants fit tighter memory budgets. All four publisher size checkpoints are available as BF16 tags. Lower-memory formats are additional choices, not replacements for those checkpoints. Tag Format Public JevBench correct Hard subset correct M5 Max resident memory¹ kev:0.8b-mlx-bf16 BF16 146 ⁄ 231 39 ⁄ 111 3.28 GiB kev:0.8b-mxfp8 MXFP8 146 ⁄ 231 39 ⁄ 111 2.84 GiB kev:4b-mlx-bf16 BF16 175 ⁄ 231 60 ⁄ 111 12.47 GiB kev:9b-mlx-bf16 BF16 184 ⁄ 231 66 ⁄ 111 19.59 GiB kev:9b-nvfp4 mixed NVFP4/MXFP8 183 ⁄ 231 68 ⁄ 111 11.16 GiB kev:27b-mlx-bf16 BF16 202 ⁄ 231 83 ⁄ 111 55.56 GiB kev:27b-nvfp4 mixed NVFP4/MXFP8 205 ⁄ 231 86 ⁄ 111 25.56 GiB ¹ /api/ps resident size after a three-question workload on one Apple M5 Max with 128 GB unified memory. It is not a peak-memory requirement. All seven JevBench rows are final-runtime local results from the same 231 public tasks in JevBench v1.2.16. Each tag returned 231 valid responses. The results do not include the 303 unavailable sealed or judge tasks and are not an official leaderboard score. Quantization changed some individual answers and probabilities even where aggregate accuracy was close. The 9B NVFP4 default answered 68 ⁄ 111 hard public tasks while using less observed resident memory than 4B BF16 ( 60 ⁄ 111 , 12.47 GiB) or 9B BF16 ( 66 ⁄ 111 , 19.59 GiB). The 27B NVFP4 tag answered 86 ⁄ 111 hard tasks and used 25.56 GiB

models.description: Readme pplx-decider is a 27B decision model from Perplexity, fine-tuned from Qwen3.8-27B. Give it a state (text, JSON, or images) and a set of typed questions, and it returns a calibrated probability for every answer in a single forward pass. It doesn’t generate text. It’s compatible with the Jev and System One APIs, so it works through Ollama’s /v1/systemone endpoint and ollama run --ask . ollama pull pplx-decider Highlights Accurate : 85.7% across 11 public benchmarks in Perplexity’s evaluation, ahead of Jev (84.5%) and its Qwen3.8-27B base (74.8%). Multimodal : decide over text, JSON, or images such as screenshots, receipts, and forms. One forward pass : every option of every question is scored together, with no output tokens. Apache 2.0 license What you can build Task You define You get back Route a request The destinations and when each applies The chosen destination and each destination’s probability Check a condition A yes or no question True or false, and the probability of each Grade an answer A rubric of levels The probability-weighted level and each level’s probability Gate an agent step A condition and the agent’s proposed action Go or no-go, with the probability of each CLI ollama run pplx-decider --ask "Is a refund being requested?" < ticket.txt ollama run pplx-decider --ask "Which team should handle this?" \ --choice billing="Payments and refunds" \ --choice technical="Outages and errors" < ticket.txt ollama run pplx-decider --ask "How urgent is this?" \ --level "Routine" \ --level "Soon" \ --level "Immediate" < ticket.txt The state can also follow the model name instead of coming from stdin. API Decision models use Ollama’s /v1/systemone endpoint, documented here . Put the text you want judged in state and your questions in questions . Ollama builds pplx-decider’s prompt for you. Field Description model pplx-decider state The text to judge. Use a string, or a JSON object or array for structured input. images Optional. Base64-encoded PNG, JPEG, or Web

models.name: Turn text, structured data, and images into scored choices, yes/no answers, and ratings.
models.description: Readme d3 is a family of decision models from vLLM Semantic Router . Give it text, structured state, or a still image, then ask it to choose a category, answer yes or no, or rate something on a scale. It returns scores and probabilities for the options you provide. It does not write a conversational answer. Use d3 to route support requests, triage documents, prioritize cases, or check whether an image meets a criterion. You can ask several questions about the same input in one request. Get started d3 runs the 4B model, a good starting point on a 16 GB machine. This example routes a support request: ollama run d3 "A customer says their card was charged twice." \ --ask "Which team should handle this?" \ --choice 'billing=Invoices and charges' \ --choice 'returns=Refunds and replacements' \ --choice 'technical=App errors' d3 requires Ollama 0.40.9 or later. Choose a size Model Best fit Tested Apple Silicon system Loaded model memory d3:2b Fast, local routing and classification 8 GB 3.62 GB d3 (4B) General use 16 GB 5.63 GB d3:9b Harder decisions that benefit from more capacity 32 GB 10.09 GB d3:27b Highest accuracy in the publisher’s family evaluation 64 GB 28.61 GB Memory figures are the peak loaded model allocations measured in Ollama for the default MXFP8 packages on Apple Silicon with a 4,096-token context. The system recommendations leave room for macOS and the full test workload. On other supported systems, these names select Q8_0 packages and memory use will differ. Format-specific tags are available when you need a particular quantization. Quality The publisher reports these Jev Decision Index 0.3.2 scores for the original checkpoints. They are not scores for the Ollama quantized packages. Model 2B 4B 9B 27B Text index 38.9 52.6 55.8 66.3 Vision index 54.7 63.2 66.9 71.3 Limits Ollama supports text, structured state, and still images for d3. Video and Box/Track decisions are unavailable. d3 scores the options and levels you supply. Clear, distinct criteria matt

models.name: d1-omni is a multimodal 600M decision model from Liquid AI
models.description: Readme d1-omni is a 600M decision model from Liquid AI, built on LFM2.5-Encoder-350M. Give it a state (text or JSON, with images or a short voice clip) and a set of typed questions, and it returns a calibrated probability for every answer in a single forward pass. It works through Ollama’s /v1/systemone endpoint and ollama run --ask . Highlights Edge-sized : 587M parameters, a 0.85 GB download. The same trunk handles every modality, with small vision (94M) and audio (112M) encoders. Images : one or more images per state; large frames are tiled. Speech : up to 30 seconds of English speech per request. One forward pass : every option of every question is scored together, with no output tokens. For the most accurate decisions over text and images, use d1 , Liquid AI’s 3B model. Use d1-omni when size matters or you need audio. Usage ollama run d1-omni --ask "Is this support request urgent?" < ticket.txt curl http://localhost:11434/v1/systemone -d '{ "model": "d1-omni", "state": "Our app crashes on launch for every user since this morning'\''s update. Please fix it now.", "questions": { "urgent": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Is this support request urgent?"}, "team": { "type": "choice", "instructions": "Which team should handle this request?", "criteria": { "billing": "Payments, invoices, and refunds", "technical": "Outages, errors, and configuration", "sales": "Plans and upgrades" } } } }' d1-omni answers urgent with 0.998 and picks technical with probability 0.995. Speech Put one base64-encoded WAV clip in images , and send audio or images, not both. Clips are cut at 30 seconds.
